item.title: AWS CloudTrail: See Who Did What in Your AWS Account
item.description: Last time I set up an alarm to be told when something goes wrong. The next question is different: who did what in my account? When a setting changes or a…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Last time I set up an alarm to be told when something goes wrong. The next question is different: who did what in my account? When a setting changes or a resource disappears, the answer comes from AWS CloudTrail.

What CloudTrail does

  • It records API activity in your account: who made the call, what they did, when, and from where.
  • That includes actions in the console, the CLI, SDKs and other AWS services.
  • It is the first place to look after a surprise change or a security question.

The building blocks

Term What it is Notes
Event One recorded API call Shows user, action, time, source IP
Event history A searchable view of recent events Management events, last 90 days, per Region
Trail A setting that delivers events to an S3 bucket Keeps history longer than 90 days
Management events Actions on resources Examples: CreateTopic, RunInstances, DeleteBucket
Data events Actions on the data inside resources Examples: S3 object reads, Lambda invokes. Off by default

Event history or a trail?

  • Event history is on by default, needs no setup and covers the last 90 days of management events.
  • A trail stores events in S3 so you can keep them, search them later and share them across the organization.
  • A trail can apply to all Regions, so activity in a Region you never use still gets recorded.

Hands-on: find who did something

  1. Open CloudTrail, then Event history.
  2. Filter by Event name and search for CreateTopic. That is the SNS topic from my last post.
  3. Open the event and read the user name, event time and source IP address.
  4. Create a trail: choose Create trail, name it management-events, let it create a new S3 bucket, and keep Management events selected.
  5. Turn on Apply trail to all Regions.
  6. Check it from the CLI: aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=CreateTopic --max-results 5

Common mistakes

  • Treating Event history as permanent when it only keeps 90 days.
  • Creating a trail for one Region only.
  • Turning on data events everywhere without thinking about cost.
  • Leaving the log bucket open to more people than needed.

Key takeaways

  • CloudTrail answers who did what, when and from where.
  • Event history is free and quick, a trail keeps the history.
  • Use a trail that covers all Regions.
  • Protect the bucket that holds the logs.

Tomorrow I'll look at AWS Config, which tracks how your resources looked over time.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Decisions and Loops Cheat Sheet: Branching, Looping and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Almost every real flow is built from two elements: a Decision that chooses a path and a Loop that works through a list. Admin II interviews love them…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Almost every real flow is built from two elements: a Decision that chooses a path and a Loop that works through a list. Admin II interviews love them, especially the rule about what never goes inside a loop.

The Two Elements at a Glance

Element What it does Key point
Decision Sends the flow down one path Outcomes are checked in order, first match wins
Default outcome The path when no outcome matches Always plan for it
Loop Goes through a collection one item at a time Has a For Each path and an After Last Item path
Assignment Changes variable values Use it inside the loop to build a collection

Interview Q&A

1. How does a Decision pick a path?

It checks its outcomes from top to bottom and takes the first one whose conditions are met. If none match, the Default outcome runs.

Tip: Put the most specific outcome first.

2. Can an outcome have several conditions?

Yes. Combine them with AND, OR or a custom logic such as 1 AND (2 OR 3).

Tip: Name outcomes clearly, for example "Has open tasks".

3. What does a Loop need?

A collection variable to loop over. The loop gives you one record at a time as the current item.

Tip: Name the loop after what it holds, such as Loop_Tasks.

4. What are the two paths out of a Loop?

For Each Item runs once per record. After Last Item runs once when the loop is done.

Tip: Do the saving after the last item, not during the loop.

5. What should you never put inside a loop?

Create, Update, Delete or Get Records elements. They run once per item and can hit governor limits.

Tip: Collect changes in a collection, then save once after the loop.

6. How do you change records in a loop the right way?

Use an Assignment to set the field on the current item, then add the item to a second collection. After the loop, run one Update Records on that collection.

Tip: Check the collection is not empty before the update.

Scenario Question

"Close all open Tasks on an Account when the rep clicks a button."

  1. Get Records for open Tasks on the Account, storing all records
  2. A Decision checks that at least one Task was found
  3. A Loop goes through the Tasks, with an Assignment that sets Status to Completed and adds the Task to a collection
  4. After the last item, one Update Records saves the collection

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create a Screen Flow with a Text variable recordId, available for input.
  2. Add Get Records on Task where WhatId equals {!recordId} and IsClosed is False. Store all records.
  3. Add a Decision with an outcome "Found tasks" where the Get Records result Is Null equals False.
  4. Create a record collection variable TasksToUpdate for Task.
  5. Add a Loop over the Get Records result. Inside it, add an Assignment that sets {!Loop_Tasks.Status} to Completed, then adds {!Loop_Tasks} to {!TasksToUpdate}.
  6. After the last item, add Update Records using {!TasksToUpdate}, and a closing screen.
  7. Run Debug on an Account with open Tasks and check the Tasks are completed.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Pick a path = Decision
  • Order = Top to bottom, first match
  • No match = Default outcome
  • One at a time = Loop
  • Save once = After Last Item
  • Never in a loop = Records elements

Key Takeaways

  • A Decision takes the first matching outcome.
  • A Loop works on one record at a time.
  • Collect changes in a collection inside the loop.
  • Save once after the last item.

Next up: Flow resources: variables, constants and formulas.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Which do you use more, Decisions or Loops? Tell me below.

item.title: I built a GitOps pipeline from scratch (Jenkins, ArgoCD, Terraform, EKS), and what broke
item.description: I wanted one project where a git push ends up as a running pod with no manual steps, then the same thing on real AWS. Here is what I built and what went…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
I wanted one project where a git push ends up as a running pod with no manual steps, then the same thing on real AWS. Here is what I built and what went wrong.

The flow

  1. I push a change to GitHub.
  2. Jenkins notices it by polling (every 2 minutes), builds a Docker image and pushes it to Docker Hub.
  3. Jenkins commits the new image tag into k8s/deployment.yaml.
  4. ArgoCD sees the manifest change and syncs it to Kubernetes.

I proved it by changing the page heading and watching the new text appear without touching anything after the push. Repo: https://github.com/RobinSishodia/aws-eks-gitops-argocd

Terraform and EKS

I rebuilt the cluster on AWS with Terraform: a VPC with public and private subnets and a NAT gateway, plus an EKS cluster with a managed node group. ArgoCD ran on it with the app Synced and Healthy. Then I destroyed all 56 resources, verified nothing was left, and deleted the access key.

What went wrong

  1. Jenkins rebuilt its own commits. The pipeline pushes a commit, so auto-triggering would loop forever. I added a guard that skips any build whose latest commit says [skip ci]. Jenkins core does not honour that tag by itself. I also once put that exact text in my own commit message and skipped a build I wanted.
  2. AWS Free plan instance types. t3.medium was rejected as not free-tier eligible. I queried the eligible types and switched to c7i-flex.large.
  3. Nodes that never joined. The EKS Terraform module does not install vpc-cni, kube-proxy or CoreDNS by default, so the nodes had no networking and the node group hung for hours. Declaring the add-ons fixed it. I also added a 25-minute create timeout so a stuck build fails fast.

What I would do next

A real GitHub webhook instead of polling (it needs Jenkins reachable from the internet), then monitoring with Prometheus and Grafana.

item.title: AWS CloudWatch Alarms and SNS: Get Notified When Something Goes Wrong
item.description: In the last two posts I set up several accounts and a way for people to sign in. Now the question every real environment hits: when something goes wrong…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
In the last two posts I set up several accounts and a way for people to sign in. Now the question every real environment hits: when something goes wrong, who finds out, and how fast? The basic answer on AWS is a CloudWatch alarm that sends a message through Amazon SNS.

What each service does

  • Amazon CloudWatch collects metrics, such as CPU use or estimated charges, and can watch them with alarms.
  • CloudWatch alarm compares a metric to a threshold and moves between three states: OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA.
  • Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service) sends a message to everyone subscribed to a topic, by email, SMS or other targets.

The building blocks

Term What it is Notes
Metric A number measured over time Example: CPUUtilization or EstimatedCharges
Alarm A rule on one metric Threshold, period and number of periods
SNS topic A channel for messages Alarms publish to it
Subscription Who receives the topic An email subscription must be confirmed
Alarm action What the alarm does on a state change Often: publish to an SNS topic

Why a topic and not a direct email

  • One topic can notify a whole team, and you can add people without touching the alarm.
  • The same topic can be reused by many alarms.
  • Later you can add other targets, such as a chat tool or a Lambda function.

Hands-on: a billing alert in your own account

  1. Sign in with a user that can open the Billing console, and turn on Receive CloudWatch billing alerts in Billing preferences.
  2. Switch the Region to US East (N. Virginia), because billing metrics are only published there.
  3. Open SNS, create a Standard topic named billing-alerts, and add an Email subscription with your address.
  4. Open the email and choose Confirm subscription. Until you do, nothing is delivered.
  5. Open CloudWatch, then Alarms, then Create alarm. Select the metric Billing > Total Estimated Charge and set a threshold such as 5 USD.
  6. For the alarm action choose In alarm, send to the billing-alerts topic, and create the alarm.
  7. Test the notification path with the CLI: aws cloudwatch set-alarm-state --alarm-name <your-alarm> --state-value ALARM --state-reason "test" and check that the email arrives.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to confirm the email subscription.
  • Creating the billing alarm in a Region other than US East (N. Virginia).
  • Setting the threshold so high that the alarm never fires.
  • Sending alerts to one personal inbox that nobody else watches.

Key takeaways

  • An alarm watches a metric, SNS delivers the message.
  • Use a topic so you can add people and targets later.
  • Confirm subscriptions and test the path on purpose.
  • Start with a billing alarm in every new account.

Tomorrow I'll look at how to see who did what in your account, with AWS CloudTrail.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Fault Paths Cheat Sheet: Handling Errors in Screen Flows and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Things go wrong, even in a good Screen Flow: a required field is empty, a record is locked, a validation rule fires. Admin II interviews ask how you handle…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Things go wrong, even in a good Screen Flow: a required field is empty, a record is locked, a validation rule fires. Admin II interviews ask how you handle it so the user sees a clear message instead of a scary error.

What Happens Without a Fault Path

If an element fails and you did nothing about it, the user sees a generic unhandled fault error and Salesforce emails the details to the admin. A fault path lets you decide what happens instead.

Idea What it means Key point
Fault connector A second path out of an element that can fail Drawn as a red dashed line
Fault message The text of the error {!$Flow.FaultMessage}
Fault screen A screen that explains the problem Shown instead of the crash
Debug Run the flow with test data Use it to trigger a failure on purpose

Interview Q&A

1. What is a fault path?

It is the path a flow takes when an element fails. You add it from the element with the Fault connector.

Tip: Think of it as the "if this fails" branch.

2. Which elements can have one?

Elements that can fail, such as Create, Update, Get and Delete Records, actions and subflows. Screen elements do not get one.

Tip: Put it on every element that changes data.

3. How do you show the error to the user?

Send the fault connector to a Screen and add a Display Text component with {!$Flow.FaultMessage}.

Tip: Add a friendly sentence above it, such as "We could not save your call."

4. Should users see the raw message?

Usually not. Raw messages can be technical. Show a plain message to the user and keep the detail for the admin.

Tip: Say what to do next, for example "Contact your admin."

5. How does the admin find out?

Salesforce sends a flow error email for unhandled faults. In your own fault path you can also send an email or create a record that logs the error.

Tip: A log record is easier to search than a pile of emails.

6. How do you test it?

Use Debug and cause a failure on purpose, such as leaving a required field empty, then check that the fault screen appears.

Tip: A fault path you never tested is a guess.

Scenario Question

"The call log flow sometimes fails and reps just see an error."

  1. Open the Screen Flow and find the Create Records element for the Task
  2. Add a Fault connector from it to a new screen
  3. Show a friendly message plus {!$Flow.FaultMessage}
  4. Debug with a failing case, then activate the new version

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Open yesterday's Screen Flow in Flow Builder.
  2. On the Create Records element that creates the Task, choose Add Fault Path.
  3. Add a Screen after it named Something went wrong.
  4. In that screen add Display Text: We could not save your call. Details: {!$Flow.FaultMessage}
  5. Run Debug and leave the Task Subject empty so the create fails.
  6. Check that the fault screen appears, then Save and Activate the new version.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Second path out = Fault connector
  • Error text = {!$Flow.FaultMessage}
  • Show it = Fault screen
  • Screens = no fault path
  • Test it = Debug a failure
  • Unhandled = Error email to admin

Key Takeaways

  • Add a fault path to every element that changes data.
  • Show a friendly message, not a crash.
  • Keep the technical detail for the admin.
  • Test the failure on purpose.

Next up: Flow decisions and loops, the two elements behind most real flows.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. How do your flows handle errors? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS IAM Identity Center: Single Sign-On Across Your AWS Accounts
item.description: Yesterday I set up an organization with several accounts. Now the next question: how do people get into those accounts without a pile of IAM users and…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday I set up an organization with several accounts. Now the next question: how do people get into those accounts without a pile of IAM users and long-term access keys? The answer is AWS IAM Identity Center.

What it does

  • It is the AWS service for workforce single sign-on across the accounts in your organization and supported applications.
  • People sign in once at the AWS access portal and pick the account and role they need.
  • Access is given through temporary credentials, so there are no long-term keys to lose.

The building blocks

Term What it is Notes
Identity source Where users and groups live Built-in directory, Active Directory or an external identity provider
Permission set A template of permissions Identity Center creates a role from it in each assigned account
Assignment Links a user or group to an account with a permission set Assign groups, not single users
Access portal The sign-in page for your users One URL for all accounts

How it fits with Organizations

  • Enable it in the management account with AWS Organizations turned on.
  • Choose the home Region carefully, because it is hard to change later.
  • Roles created from permission sets show up in each account with names starting AWSReservedSSO_.
  • Session length is set per permission set.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Open IAM Identity Center in the management account and choose Enable.
  2. Under Groups, create a group named ReadOnly, then create a user and add them to it.
  3. Under Permission sets, create one that uses the AWS managed ViewOnlyAccess or ReadOnlyAccess policy.
  4. Under AWS accounts, select an account, choose Assign users or groups, and pick the group and the permission set.
  5. Open the access portal URL, sign in as the user, and choose the account and role.
  6. Optional: run aws configure sso, then aws sso login, and check with aws sts get-caller-identity.

Common mistakes

  • Creating IAM users for every person instead of using Identity Center.
  • Assigning permission sets to single users, which gets hard to manage.
  • Giving broad access when a read-only permission set is enough.
  • Forgetting MFA for the people who sign in.

Key takeaways

  • Use Identity Center for people and IAM roles for workloads.
  • Define access once in a permission set and assign it to groups.
  • Prefer temporary credentials over long-term keys.
  • Keep MFA on for every user.

Tomorrow I'll look at what happens when something goes wrong in your accounts, starting with how to be notified.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Screen Flow Launch Cheat Sheet: Quick Actions, Lightning Pages and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: A Screen Flow only helps if users can find it. Admin II interviews ask where you would launch one, how it knows which record it is on, and who is allowed…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
A Screen Flow only helps if users can find it. Admin II interviews ask where you would launch one, how it knows which record it is on, and who is allowed to run it.

The 4 Ways to Launch a Screen Flow

Where How Key point
Quick action Action of type Flow on an object Shows as a button on the record page
Lightning page The Flow component Runs inline on the page
URL or button /flow/FlowApiName Good for links and custom buttons
Utility bar Flow utility item Always available in the app

Interview Q&A

1. Why must the flow be active?

Users can only run an active flow. Activate it before you add it to a page, an action or a link.

Tip: Test with Debug first, then activate.

2. How do you add a quick action?

In Object Manager, create an action of type Flow, pick the flow and give it a short label. Then add it to the page layout so the button appears.

Tip: Keep the label short so it fits on the button.

3. How do you embed the flow on a page?

In the Lightning App Builder, drag the Flow component onto the page and choose the flow.

Tip: One flow per section keeps the page clean.

4. How does the flow get the current record?

Create a Text variable named recordId and tick Available for input. Salesforce passes the record Id in when the flow runs from a record page.

Tip: The variable name must match exactly.

5. Who can run it?

Users need access to the flow, for example the Run Flows permission, or access given through a profile or permission set.

Tip: Test as a real user, not only as an admin.

6. What happens when the flow finishes?

Show a confirmation screen, or use the flow's finish setting to restart it or send the user elsewhere.

Tip: End with a clear message so the user knows it worked.

Scenario Question

"Let reps log a call from the Account page."

  1. Build the Screen Flow with a recordId variable
  2. Activate it
  3. Create a Flow quick action on Account
  4. Add it to the page layout and test as a rep

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Open yesterday's Screen Flow and add a Text variable recordId, available for input.
  2. Use {!recordId} as the WhatId when it creates the Task.
  3. Save and Activate the flow.
  4. In Object Manager, create a Flow quick action on Account and add it to the page layout.
  5. Open an Account, run the action, and check that the Task is linked to that Account.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Run from a record = Quick action
  • Embed inline = Flow component
  • Link to it = /flow/ApiName
  • Know the record = recordId
  • Must be = Active
  • Access = Run Flows

Key Takeaways

  • Activate before you place it.
  • Use recordId for record context.
  • Pick the launch spot that suits the user.
  • Test as a real user.

Next up: Flow error handling and fault paths in Screen Flows.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Where do your users launch Screen Flows? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS Organizations: Multiple Accounts, OUs and Service Control Policies
item.description: So far I have secured root, set a budget, turned on CloudTrail and CloudWatch, and added tags. All of that sits in one account. The next step is the…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
So far I have secured root, set a budget, turned on CloudTrail and CloudWatch, and added tags. All of that sits in one account. The next step is the structure around it: AWS Organizations.

Why more than one account

  • An AWS account is a strong boundary for security, cost and blast radius.
  • A mistake in a sandbox account cannot touch production.
  • Each account has its own root user, IAM and limits, so teams can work separately.

The building blocks

Term What it is Notes
Organization The group of accounts you manage together Created from one account
Management account The account that creates the organization and pays the bill SCPs do not apply to it
Member accounts Every other account in the organization One per workload or team
OU An organizational unit that groups accounts Policies on an OU apply to its accounts
SCP A service control policy Sets the maximum permissions, never grants them

Consolidated billing

  • All member accounts roll up to one bill on the management account.
  • Usage across accounts can count together for volume discounts.
  • Tags still let you split cost by project or owner.

How SCPs behave

  • An SCP is a guardrail: an action must be allowed by the SCP and by the identity's own IAM policy.
  • They apply to IAM users and roles in member accounts, including the account root user.
  • They do not apply to the management account, so keep workloads out of it.
  • Use all features mode to turn SCPs on.

A simple starting structure

  • Security OU: logging and audit accounts
  • Workloads OU: production and non-production accounts
  • Sandbox OU: learning and experiments, with tighter SCPs

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Open AWS Organizations and choose Create an organization.
  2. Check that MFA is on for the management account root user.
  3. Create an OU named Sandbox.
  4. Choose Add an AWS account, then Create an AWS account, and give it a unique email address and a name. Move it into the Sandbox OU.
  5. Open Policies, enable service control policies, and attach a deny policy to the Sandbox OU, for example one that stops the account leaving the organization.
  6. Sign in to the management account and assume the OrganizationAccountAccessRole in the new account to check it works.

Common mistakes

  • Running workloads in the management account.
  • Using SCPs as if they grant permissions. They only limit.
  • Reusing one email address for several accounts. Each account needs a unique one.
  • Attaching SCPs to the organization root before testing on a Sandbox OU.

Key takeaways

  • Use separate accounts as security and cost boundaries.
  • Group accounts into OUs and attach policy once.
  • SCPs set the maximum, IAM still grants.
  • Keep the management account for administration only.

Tomorrow I'll look at how people and tools sign in across these accounts.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Screens Cheat Sheet: User Input, Validation and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Screens are how a Flow talks to the user. Admin II interviews ask about them because input, validation and navigation decide whether a Screen Flow is easy…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Screens are how a Flow talks to the user. Admin II interviews ask about them because input, validation and navigation decide whether a Screen Flow is easy to use and safe to trust.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it does Key point
Input components Collect text, numbers, dates and more The value is stored for later elements
Choice components Radio buttons, picklists, checkboxes Fed by a choice or a choice set
Display components Show text, sections and messages Guide the user
Validation Required, or a formula with an error message Stops bad data early

Interview Q&A

1. What is a Screen element?

The element that shows a user interface and collects input. Screens only work in Screen Flows, not in record-triggered or autolaunched flows.

Tip: Use a Screen whenever a person has to type or choose something.

2. How do you use what the user entered?

Each screen component keeps its value. Reference it with the component's API name, for example {!Subject.value}, in later elements such as Create Records.

Tip: Give components clear API names. You will type them a lot.

3. How do you validate input?

Mark a field Required, or open its Validate Input setting and add a formula with an error message. The user cannot continue until the formula is true.

Tip: Stop bad data at the screen, not after it is saved.

4. Can you hide components?

Yes. Set Component Visibility conditions on a field or a section, so it only appears when an earlier answer calls for it.

Tip: Show only what the user needs for this case.

5. Where do choices come from?

Create a Choice resource for a fixed option, or a Record Choice Set or Picklist Choice Set to load options from records or from a field's picklist values.

Tip: Build a choice set once and reuse it across screens.

6. How does the user move through the flow?

With the Next, Previous and Finish buttons. You choose which of them each screen shows, and whether the user can go back.

Tip: Check the Back button on every screen. Going back can change data you already saved.

Scenario Question

"Let sales reps log a call from a Screen Flow."

  1. Screen: Subject (text), Priority (picklist), Due Date (date)
  2. Create Records: a Task, with fields from the screen inputs
  3. Confirmation screen that shows the new Task Id
  4. Fault path on Create Records, then Debug

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create a Screen Flow and add a Screen with a Text input named Subject.
  2. Add a Picklist choice for Priority and a Date input for Due Date.
  3. Make Subject Required, and add a Validate formula so the date cannot be in the past.
  4. Add Create Records for Task and map the three inputs.
  5. Add a confirmation screen, run Debug, then add the flow to a Lightning page.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Show UI = Screen
  • Read input = {!Name.value}
  • Block bad data = Validate Input
  • Hide fields = Component Visibility
  • Pick from a list = Choice or choice set
  • Save the data = Create Records after the screen

Key Takeaways

  • Screens belong to Screen Flows.
  • Validate on the screen.
  • Reuse choice sets.
  • Save once, after the user is done.

Next up: running a Screen Flow from buttons, Lightning pages and quick actions.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Which Screen component do you use most? Tell me below.

item.title: I built a tiny GitHub repo auditor, and it found my own mess
item.description: Just shipped repo-health-report: a tiny, dependency-free Python tool that audits your GitHub repos through the REST API. It flags missing licenses…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Just shipped repo-health-report: a tiny, dependency-free Python tool that audits your GitHub repos through the REST API.

It flags missing licenses, descriptions, topics and READMEs, plus pull requests that have gone stale. It also runs as a scheduled GitHub Action and writes the results to the job summary.

On my own account it found 15 repos without a license. I fixed 12 of them in an afternoon.

What it checks

  • Missing license
  • Missing description or topics
  • Missing README
  • Open pull requests with no activity for 30+ days

Try it

python repo_health_report.py <github-username>

Code and setup: https://github.com/RobinSishodia/repo-health-report

Feedback and issues welcome. If it's useful to you, a star helps.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Formulas Cheat Sheet: Dates, Booleans and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: A Flow formula calculates a value from your data and variables, so you can skip extra Decision and Assignment elements. Admin II interviews ask about them…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
A Flow formula calculates a value from your data and variables, so you can skip extra Decision and Assignment elements. Admin II interviews ask about them because formulas keep Flows small, readable and easy to maintain.

Formula Basics

Piece What it does Key point
Formula resource Returns one calculated value Created under New Resource
Data type Text, Number, Currency, Date, Date/Time or Boolean Pick the type the formula returns
Functions IF, AND, OR, TEXT, TODAY, BLANKVALUE and more Same style as validation rule formulas
Where you use it Decision conditions, Assignments, Screen text, Get Records filters Reference it like a variable

Interview Q&A

1. What is a formula resource in a Flow?

A resource that calculates one value from fields, variables and functions, then returns it. Reference it anywhere you would use a variable.

Tip: One formula, used in many places.

2. Why use a formula instead of Decision and Assignment elements?

A formula can do the same logic in one resource, such as a calculated date or a yes/no flag. The Flow canvas stays short and readable.

Tip: Fewer elements, fewer places to break.

3. How do you handle blank values?

Use BLANKVALUE or ISBLANK (or ISNULL checks in conditions) so a missing field does not break the result. Empty values in math can lead to unexpected results.

Tip: Always plan for blank.

4. Can a formula return a Boolean?

Yes. A Boolean formula returns true or false, which is handy as a single condition in a Decision, for example whether an Opportunity amount is over a limit and the stage is open.

Tip: Boolean formula in, simple Decision out.

5. How do you use dates in a formula?

Use TODAY() or NOW() and add or subtract days, for example TODAY() + 7 for a follow-up date. Pick Date or Date/Time to match the field you set.

Tip: Match the formula type to the field type.

6. Where are the limits?

A formula returns one value, it cannot change records, and it cannot query other records directly. Use Get Records for data, then use the formula to work with it.

Tip: Get Records finds, formulas calculate.

Scenario Question

"Create a follow-up Task due in 7 days, or 2 days if the Opportunity is over 100,000."

  1. Record-triggered flow on Opportunity, after save, when Stage becomes Negotiation
  2. Formula (Date): IF({!$Record.Amount} > 100000, TODAY() + 2, TODAY() + 7)
  3. Create Records: a Task with ActivityDate set to the formula
  4. Fault path, then Debug

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create a Screen Flow with a Number input for an amount.
  2. Add a Formula resource of type Text that returns IF({!Amount} > 1000, "High", "Normal").
  3. Add a Screen that displays the formula result.
  4. Add a second Formula of type Date that returns TODAY() + 7 and show that too.
  5. Run Debug with a few amounts and check the results.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Formula = one calculated value
  • Boolean formula = single true or false condition
  • Date formula = TODAY() plus or minus days
  • Blank safe = BLANKVALUE or ISBLANK
  • Cannot = change records or query data
  • Pair with = Get Records for data

Key Takeaways

  • Use a formula to replace small Decision and Assignment chains.
  • Match the formula data type to what it feeds.
  • Plan for blank values.
  • Get Records finds data, formulas calculate on it.

Next up: Flow screens and user input.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. What is the most useful Flow formula you have written? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS Tagging Strategy: Name, Owner and Environment Tags for Every Resource
item.description: By now I have IAM, a budget, CloudTrail and CloudWatch. One more habit makes all of them easier to use: tags. When the bill rises or something looks odd…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
By now I have IAM, a budget, CloudTrail and CloudWatch. One more habit makes all of them easier to use: tags. When the bill rises or something looks odd, tags tell you what the resource is, who owns it and what it is for.

What tags are

  • A tag is a key and value pair attached to a resource, such as Environment = dev.
  • Most AWS resources support tags, and you can have up to 50 tags per resource.
  • Tags are labels for people and tools. They do not change how the resource works.

A simple starting set

Key Example value Why
Name web-server-1 Shows in the console list
Environment dev, test, prod Separate workloads
Owner robin Who to ask
Project blog-site Group related resources
CostCenter learning Split the bill

What tags are used for

  • Cost allocation: activate cost allocation tags in Billing, then filter Cost Explorer by tag.
  • Access control: IAM policies can allow or deny actions based on tags (ABAC).
  • Automation: scripts can find resources by tag, such as all Environment = dev instances to stop at night.
  • Search: Tag Editor and Resource Groups find resources across Regions.

Good to know

  • Tag keys and values are case sensitive, so Owner and owner are different.
  • Tags are not retroactive in Cost Explorer. Cost allocation tags only show costs from the time you activate them.
  • Tag policies in AWS Organizations help keep names consistent.
  • Do not put secrets or personal data in tags.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Open EC2 or S3 and select a resource you created.
  2. Add the tags Name, Environment, Owner and Project.
  3. Open Resource Groups & Tag Editor and use Tag Editor to search by Environment = dev across Regions.
  4. Open Billing and Cost allocation tags, then activate Project.
  5. After a day, filter Cost Explorer by the Project tag.

Common mistakes

  • Inconsistent keys, such as env, Env and Environment.
  • Tagging only some resources, so reports have gaps.
  • Forgetting to activate cost allocation tags.
  • Storing sensitive data in tag values.

Key takeaways

  • Tags answer what, who and why for every resource.
  • Pick a small standard set and use it everywhere.
  • Activate cost allocation tags to see costs by tag.
  • Keep tag names consistent.

Tomorrow I'll look at how to see all of this from a single place: AWS Organizations and account structure.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Loop Element Cheat Sheet: Bulk-Safe Collections and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: The Loop element lets a Flow work through a collection one record at a time. Admin II interviews ask about it because loops are where Flows either stay…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
The Loop element lets a Flow work through a collection one record at a time. Admin II interviews ask about it because loops are where Flows either stay bulk-safe or hit governor limits.

The 4 Loop Pieces

Piece What it does Key point
Collection variable Holds the records to process Often from Get Records
Loop element Hands you one item at a time Exposes the current item variable
Assignment inside Changes the current item or builds an output collection No DML here
Data element after Saves the output collection once One Update Records outside the loop

Interview Q&A

1. What does the Loop element do?

It goes through a collection and gives you one item at a time as a loop variable. It has two paths: For Each Item runs for every item, and After Last Item runs once at the end.

Tip: Put the save step on After Last Item.

2. Why not put Update Records inside the loop?

Each pass would run one DML call. With many records you hit governor limits and the Flow fails. Instead, add each changed item to a second collection, then update that collection once after the loop.

Tip: Never put DML or Get Records inside a loop.

3. How do you change a field on the current item?

Use an Assignment inside the loop to set the field on the loop variable, then add the loop variable to an output collection.

Tip: Loop variable in, output collection out.

4. Can you loop in reverse?

Yes. The Loop element has a direction setting: first to last or last to first.

Tip: Use reverse when order matters.

5. When can you skip the loop?

Often a Flow does not need one. Update Records with conditions can change every matching record in a single element, and a before-save flow can set fields on the triggering record directly.

Tip: No loop is the safest loop.

6. How do you debug a loop?

Run Debug and watch the loop variable change on each pass. Use the Flow's fault path and, for large data, test with a small set first.

Tip: Test with 2 records, then 200.

Scenario Question

"Set every open Opportunity on an Account to Needs Review when the Account is marked At Risk."

  1. Record-triggered flow on Account, after save, when At_Risk__c becomes true
  2. Get Records: open Opportunities where AccountId equals the Account Id
  3. Loop through them, with an Assignment setting StageName and adding each to an output collection
  4. Update Records on the output collection, once, after the loop

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create a Screen Flow and add Get Records for a few Contacts into a collection.
  2. Add a Loop over that collection.
  3. Inside the loop, add an Assignment that sets the current Contact's Description, then adds it to a new collection.
  4. After the last item, add Update Records using the new collection.
  5. Run Debug and check the Contacts in your org.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Loop = one item at a time
  • For Each Item = runs per record
  • After Last Item = runs once at the end
  • Output collection = what you save
  • DML = outside the loop
  • Often no loop = Update Records with conditions

Key Takeaways

  • Loop through a collection, build an output collection, save once.
  • Never put DML or Get Records inside a loop.
  • Skip the loop when one element can do the job.
  • Test with small data first.

Next up: Flow formulas and how they replace small pieces of logic.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Do you try to avoid loops, or use them often? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS CloudWatch Basics: Metrics, Logs and Alarms for Your Resources
item.description: Last time I looked at who changed things with CloudTrail. The next question is different: what is happening inside my resources right now? That is Amazon…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Last time I looked at who changed things with CloudTrail. The next question is different: what is happening inside my resources right now? That is Amazon CloudWatch.

What CloudWatch does

  • Metrics: numbers over time, such as EC2 CPU utilization or S3 request counts.
  • Logs: log data from your applications and services, stored in log groups.
  • Alarms: watch a metric and do something when it crosses a threshold.
  • Dashboards: put the graphs you care about on one page.

CloudTrail vs CloudWatch

Question Service
Who made this change? CloudTrail
Is this resource healthy and busy? CloudWatch

How an alarm works

  • An alarm watches one metric over a period (for example, 5 minutes).
  • Its state is OK, ALARM or INSUFFICIENT_DATA.
  • When the state changes, it can send a message to an SNS topic, which can email you.
  • The threshold and the number of periods to evaluate decide how sensitive it is.

Good to know

  • EC2 sends basic metrics every 5 minutes by default, and detailed monitoring gives 1-minute data (extra cost).
  • EC2 does not report memory or disk usage by default. You need the CloudWatch agent for those.
  • Logs stay forever unless you set a retention period, so set one.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Open CloudWatch and browse All metrics for EC2 or S3.
  2. Choose Alarms, then Create alarm.
  3. Pick a metric, such as EC2 CPUUtilization for one instance.
  4. Set a threshold, for example greater than 70% for 2 periods.
  5. Create or choose an SNS topic with your email, and confirm the subscription email.
  6. Save the alarm and check that it shows OK or INSUFFICIENT_DATA at first.

Common mistakes

  • Creating alarms with no action, so nobody is told.
  • Forgetting to confirm the SNS email subscription.
  • Expecting memory metrics without the CloudWatch agent.
  • Leaving log groups on never-expire retention.

Key takeaways

  • CloudTrail tells you who changed it, CloudWatch tells you how it is doing.
  • Metrics feed alarms, alarms feed SNS, SNS reaches you.
  • Install the agent for memory and disk.
  • Set log retention.

Tomorrow I'll look at how to use tags to keep resources organized and costs traceable.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Create, Update and Delete Records Cheat Sheet: Fault Paths and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Create Records, Update Records and Delete Records are how a Flow changes data. Admin II interviews ask about them because small choices here decide whether…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Create Records, Update Records and Delete Records are how a Flow changes data. Admin II interviews ask about them because small choices here decide whether a Flow is safe, fast and bulk-ready.

The 3 Data Elements

Element What it does Key point
Create Records Adds new records Can store the new record Id
Update Records Changes existing records Filter, or pass a record or collection
Delete Records Removes records Use filters or a collection, and be careful

Interview Q&A

1. How does Create Records set field values?

Either set the fields one by one, or use all values from a record variable or collection you built earlier. Choose Create multiple records when you pass a collection.

Tip: Build a collection, then create once.

2. How can Update Records pick what to change?

Two ways: specify conditions and set fields individually, or use the Ids and all field values from a record or collection. The first changes every record that matches the filter.

Tip: Check the filter before you run it.

3. Why store the new record Id?

After Create Records you can store the Id in a variable. Use it to create related records, such as a Task linked to the new Case.

Tip: Store the Id, then relate children to it.

4. How do you make a Flow bulk-safe?

Do the work on a collection: add records to it in the loop with an Assignment, and run one Create, Update or Delete Records after the loop.

Tip: DML belongs outside the loop.

5. What is a fault path?

A fault connector that runs when a data element fails, for example on a validation rule error. Use it to show a message or log the error.

Tip: Add a fault path to every data element.

6. Update Records or an Assignment on $Record?

In a before-save record-triggered flow, an Assignment on $Record changes the record with no extra DML. In an after-save flow, use Update Records to change the triggering record or related records.

Tip: Before-save is faster for same-record updates.

Scenario Question

"When a Case is closed, create a follow-up Task and mark the related Contact as contacted."

  1. Record-triggered flow on Case, after save, when Status changes to Closed
  2. Create Records: a Task, with WhatId set to the Case Id
  3. Update Records: set the Contact's Last_Contacted__c field
  4. Fault path on both elements, then Debug

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create a Screen Flow with a text input for a Case subject.
  2. Add Create Records for Case, set Subject from the input, and store the new Id in a variable.
  3. Add Update Records that sets the same Case's Priority to High using that Id.
  4. Add a fault path from each element to a screen that shows {!$Flow.FaultMessage}.
  5. Run Debug and check the new Case in your org.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Add = Create Records
  • Change = Update Records
  • Remove = Delete Records
  • Many at once = collection, one element after the loop
  • Failure = fault path
  • Same record, before save = Assignment on $Record

Key Takeaways

  • Work on collections, then save once.
  • Store the Id to build related records.
  • Add a fault path to every data element.
  • Be careful with filters on Update and Delete.

Next up: the Loop element and how to process collections safely.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Which data element do you use most? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS CloudTrail Basics: Who Did What, When and From Where
item.description: This week I locked the root account and set a budget. Now the question that comes after both: when something changes in the account, how do I find out who…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
This week I locked the root account and set a budget. Now the question that comes after both: when something changes in the account, how do I find out who did it, what they did and when? That is AWS CloudTrail.

What CloudTrail records

  • CloudTrail logs API activity in your account, whether it came from the console, the CLI, an SDK or another AWS service.
  • Each event says who (the identity), what (the API call), when, and where from (the source IP address).
  • It is the audit trail you open when a resource disappears or a setting changes.

Event types

Type What it covers Notes
Management events Control-plane actions, such as creating a role or launching an instance Recorded by default
Data events Object-level actions, such as S3 object reads or Lambda invokes Off by default, extra cost
Insights events Unusual API activity Optional

Event history vs a trail

  • Event history is on by default and lets you look up recent management events (the last 90 days) in the console, with no setup.
  • A trail delivers events to an S3 bucket (and optionally CloudWatch Logs) so you keep them longer and can search them with other tools.
  • A multi-Region trail records activity in all Regions, so nothing slips through in a Region you do not use.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Open CloudTrail and choose Event history.
  2. Filter by Event name ConsoleLogin and open one event to see who signed in and from which IP address.
  3. Filter by User name root to check whether root has been used, tying back to the root account checklist.
  4. Choose Create trail, name it, and create or choose an S3 bucket for the logs.
  5. Enable a multi-Region trail and log file validation, then create it.
  6. After a few minutes, open the S3 bucket and find the delivered log files.

Common mistakes

  • Relying on event history only, then needing events older than 90 days.
  • Creating a trail in one Region and missing activity elsewhere.
  • Leaving the log bucket open. Keep it private.
  • Turning on data events everywhere without checking the cost.

Key takeaways

  • CloudTrail answers who, what, when and from where.
  • Event history is free to browse, a trail keeps the records.
  • Use a multi-Region trail and keep the bucket private.
  • Check root activity regularly.

Tomorrow I'll look at how to see what is happening inside your resources, not just who changed them.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Get Records Cheat Sheet: Filters, Sort Order, Null Checks and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Get Records is how a Flow reads data. Admin II interviews ask about its filters, sort order and null checks because a badly built one is the most common…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Get Records is how a Flow reads data. Admin II interviews ask about its filters, sort order and null checks because a badly built one is the most common cause of slow or broken Flows.

The 4 Settings That Matter

Setting What it controls Key point
Filter conditions Which records come back AND, OR or custom logic
Sort order Which record is "first" Set it whenever you need one record
How many records One or many Only the first record, or all records
Store fields What data is kept Choose only the fields you need

Interview Q&A

1. How do you filter a Get Records?

Add filter conditions on the object's fields, such as Status Equals Open. Combine them with All Conditions Are Met (AND), Any Condition Is Met (OR) or Custom Condition Logic.

Tip: Filter in Get Records, not after it.

2. Why does sort order matter?

With Only the first record, Salesforce returns the first match in your sort order. Without a sort, which record you get is not guaranteed.

Tip: Sort by CreatedDate descending for "latest".

3. One record or all records?

Only the first record stores a single record variable. All records stores a collection you can loop over.

Tip: Match the choice to the variable you need.

4. Which fields should you store?

Choose only the fields you need instead of all fields. Fewer fields means less data to carry through the Flow.

Tip: Name the fields you will actually read.

5. What if no record is found?

The variable is empty (null). Add a Decision after the Get Records that checks whether the variable Is Null, and handle that path.

Tip: Always plan the "found nothing" path.

6. Why keep Get Records out of loops?

Each Get Records is a SOQL query, and a transaction has a limit on queries. A query inside a loop can hit that limit on bulk data.

Tip: Query once before the loop, then loop the collection.

Scenario Question

"A flow must find the most recent open Case for a Contact and show its subject."

  1. Get Records on Case: ContactId Equals the Contact AND Status Does Not Equal Closed
  2. Sort by CreatedDate descending, Only the first record
  3. Decision: is the Case variable Is Null?
  4. Display the Subject, or a "No open cases" message

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create a Screen Flow and add a Get Records element on Case, returning Only the first record.
  2. Add a filter Status Does Not Equal Closed and sort by CreatedDate descending.
  3. Choose Choose fields and let Salesforce do the rest and pick Subject and Status.
  4. Add a Decision that checks the Case variable Is Null and a screen for each path.
  5. Run Debug with a Contact who has open cases and one who has none.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Read data = Get Records
  • Narrow it down = filter conditions
  • Pick the first = sort order
  • A list = All records (collection)
  • Nothing found = Is Null Decision
  • Efficiency = store only needed fields, no queries in loops

Key Takeaways

  • Filter and sort inside Get Records.
  • Always handle the nothing-found path.
  • Store only the fields you need.
  • Query once, then loop.

Next up: Update Records and Create Records, and how they save changes.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Which Get Records setting trips you up? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS Budgets and Billing Alerts: Set a Spending Limit Before You Build
item.description: Yesterday I locked down the root account and noted "keep billing alerts up to date". Today is the other half of the front door: making sure a forgotten…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday I locked down the root account and noted "keep billing alerts up to date". Today is the other half of the front door: making sure a forgotten resource never turns into a surprise bill. AWS Budgets does that.

What AWS Budgets does

  • You set a spending limit (or a usage limit) and AWS compares your actual and forecasted spend against it.
  • When a threshold is crossed, it emails you (and can notify an SNS topic).
  • Spend data is not instant. Billing data can lag, so treat alerts as an early warning, not a live meter.

Types of budget

Type Tracks Good for
Cost budget Dollars spent Almost every learner
Usage budget Units used, such as hours or GB Watching a specific service
Savings Plans / Reservation budgets Coverage and utilization Later, when you commit to spend

Two templates to start with

  • Zero spend budget: alerts you as soon as your spend goes above the free tier. Ideal for a learning account.
  • Monthly cost budget: you choose a monthly amount, and the console sets alerts at 85% of actual spend, 100% of actual spend and 100% of forecasted spend.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Sign in and open Billing and Cost Management, then Budgets.
  2. Choose Create budget and pick a template, such as Zero spend budget or Monthly cost budget.
  3. Name it, set the amount (for example 10 USD) and add the email addresses to alert.
  4. Review the thresholds and create the budget.
  5. Optionally, as the root user, turn on IAM user and role access to Billing information so your admin identity can see costs without using root.

Common mistakes

  • Creating a budget but typing the email address wrongly.
  • Setting only an actual-spend alert, so you hear about a problem after the money is gone.
  • Forgetting that some services keep charging until you delete the resource.
  • Using root every time to check the bill instead of enabling billing access for IAM.

Worth knowing next

Cost Explorer shows where your spend comes from, and Cost Anomaly Detection can flag unusual spikes. Budgets tells you that spend is rising. Those two help explain why.

Key takeaways

  • Create a budget before you create any real resources.
  • Alert on forecasted spend as well as actual spend.
  • Give billing access to an IAM admin, not just root.
  • Delete what you stop using.

Tomorrow I'll go one step further into securing access to the account.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Decision and Assignment Elements Cheat Sheet: Outcomes, Operators and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Decisions send a flow down the right path. Assignments change values along the way. Admin II interviews ask about both because almost every real Flow uses…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Decisions send a flow down the right path. Assignments change values along the way. Admin II interviews ask about both because almost every real Flow uses them.

The 2 Elements

Element What it does Key point
Decision Routes the flow into one path Outcomes are checked top to bottom, the first match wins
Assignment Sets or changes values Changes variables, not the database

Interview Q&A

1. How does a Decision pick a path?

It checks its outcomes from top to bottom. The first outcome whose conditions are met runs. If none match, the Default Outcome runs.

Tip: Put the most specific outcome first.

2. How can outcome conditions be combined?

Choose All Conditions Are Met (AND), Any Condition Is Met (OR), Custom Logic such as 1 AND (2 OR 3), or Always (No Conditions Required).

Tip: Use custom logic for mixed AND and OR.

3. What does an Assignment do?

It sets values on variables, including fields of a record variable such as {!caseRecord.Status}. Operators include Equals, Add and Subtract.

Tip: Equals overwrites, Add accumulates.

4. Does an Assignment save to the database?

No. It only changes values in the flow. Use Update Records to save, except for $Record in a before-save record-triggered flow, which saves automatically.

Tip: Assignment edits, Update Records saves.

5. How do you build up a collection?

Use an Assignment on a collection variable with the Add operator to put each record in the list. Then use one Update Records after the loop.

Tip: Never put DML inside a loop.

6. What should the Default Outcome do?

Handle everything no outcome matched. Rename it so the path is clear, and leave it connected to something, even a simple end.

Tip: Plan the "none of the above" case.

Scenario Question

"A record-triggered flow must escalate high-priority Cases from Premium accounts."

  1. Decision: Priority equals High AND account type is Premium
  2. Assignment: set Escalated to true and Status to Escalated on {!caseRecord}
  3. Assignment: add the record to a collection
  4. One Update Records after the loop, then Debug

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create a Screen Flow with a Get Records for one Case into a record variable.
  2. Add a Decision with an outcome High Priority where Priority equals High, and leave the Default Outcome as Other.
  3. On the High Priority path, add an Assignment that sets {!caseRecord.Status} to Escalated.
  4. Add an Update Records element that saves {!caseRecord}.
  5. Run Debug with a High priority Case and then a Low priority Case, and compare the paths.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Choose a path = Decision
  • Change a value = Assignment
  • Order of outcomes = top to bottom
  • None matched = Default Outcome
  • Save changes = Update Records
  • Add to a list = Assignment on a collection

Key Takeaways

  • Decisions route, Assignments change values.
  • The first matching outcome wins.
  • Assignments do not save to the database.
  • Keep DML outside loops.

Next up: the Get Records element and how filters and sort order work.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Which element do you use most? Tell me below.

item.title: Protect the AWS Root Account and Turn on MFA
item.description: Every AWS account starts with one identity that can do everything: the root user. IAM policies cannot restrict it, so if someone gets in, there is no…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Every AWS account starts with one identity that can do everything: the root user. IAM policies cannot restrict it, so if someone gets in, there is no safety net. Before building anything else, lock it down.

What the root user is (and is not)

  • It is the email address you signed up with, and it has unrestricted access to the whole account, including billing and closing the account.
  • It is not an IAM user, so you cannot limit it with a policy.
  • You should almost never sign in with it. Daily work belongs to IAM identities (Day 1) and roles (Day 3).

The root account checklist

Step Why it matters
Turn on MFA for the root user A stolen password alone is no longer enough
Use a long, unique password in a password manager Root should not share a password with anything else
Delete root access keys (or never create them) A leaked key would have full power with no MFA prompt
Use a shared mailbox or alias you control You keep recovery access if one person leaves
Keep alternate contacts and billing alerts up to date You hear about problems early

Choosing an MFA type

  • Passkey or security key (FIDO2): phishing-resistant, the strongest everyday option.
  • Authenticator app (TOTP): free, quick to set up, and fine for most learners.
  • Hardware TOTP token: a physical code generator, mostly for strict environments.

You can register more than one MFA device on the same user, so add a second one as a backup.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Sign in as the root user, open the account menu and choose Security credentials.
  2. Under Multi-factor authentication (MFA), choose Assign MFA device.
  3. Give it a clear name, pick Authenticator app or Passkey or security key, and follow the prompts.
  4. Under Access keys, confirm there are none. If there are, delete them.
  5. Sign out and sign in again to confirm the MFA prompt appears.
  6. Create an IAM admin identity for daily use and stop using root.

Common mistakes

  • Using root for everyday tasks "just this once".
  • Keeping root access keys in a script or a laptop folder.
  • Registering MFA on a single phone with no backup device.
  • Using a personal inbox that only one person can read.

What only root can do

A short list of tasks still needs root, such as changing the account name or email, closing the account and restoring IAM permissions if you lock yourself out. That is the only reason to sign in as root.

Key takeaways

  • The root user is unrestricted, so protect it before anything else.
  • Turn on MFA, remove access keys and keep a backup MFA device.
  • Do real work with IAM users and roles, not root.

Tomorrow I'll look at what comes next once the front door is locked.
